title: Uutissuomalainen: Several researchers have requested the Tiitinen list for their use, including emeritus professor Alpo Rusi
originalSummary: Suojelupoliisi ei ole toistaiseksi vastannut tutkimuspyyntöihin. Supon mukaan hakemusten käsittelyaika on noin 6–12 kuukautta.
analysis:
According to a report by Uutissuomalainen, the Finnish Security Intelligence Service (Supo) has received requests from three researchers and one research group at the end of last year or the beginning of this year, seeking access to the so-called Tiitinen list. Among the members of the requesting research group are emeritus professor Alpo Rusi and journalist Pekka Virkki, while Supo has withheld the name of one of the inquiring researchers. Supo has not yet responded to the requests, noting that the processing time typically takes between six to 12 months. In November, Supo's director Juha Martelius indicated that the agency might grant access to the list for relevant research purposes. The Tiitinen list refers to a document received in 1990 by then-head of Supo, Seppo Tiitinen, containing the names of 18 Finns suspected of having had contact with the East German intelligence service, Stasi. Historically, Alpo Rusi was himself suspected by Supo of aggravated espionage on behalf of East Germany, a pre-trial investigation that leaked to the public, though it never resulted in charges and the Finnish state was subsequently ordered to pay damages to Rusi. 

The question of whether to grant access to historical intelligence archives touches upon a fundamental tension in democratic governance: the balance between protecting state security methods, privacy, and institutional reputation versus fulfilling the public's right to historical transparency and accountability. From a policy perspective, withholding historical documents indefinitely can foster public distrust in security institutions, particularly when those institutions were involved in controversial investigations involving domestic political figures. However, intelligence agencies operate on the premise of protecting sources and maintaining operational integrity, principles that traditionally extend even to historical files to prevent setting precedents that could compromise contemporary intelligence-sharing relationships. In the case of the Tiitinen list, where decades have passed and the geopolitical context of the Cold War has entirely dissolved, the necessity of absolute secrecy weakens considerably. Keeping such lists under lock and foot fosters speculation and harms the reputations of individuals who were merely listed without formal charges being proven, as demonstrated by the case of Alpo Rusi. Transparency, therefore, serves as a mechanism for historical closure and institutional rehabilitation.

To address this ongoing controversy constructively, the Finnish Security Intelligence Service should adopt a formalized, transparent framework for evaluating requests for historical archives that are no longer sensitive for national security. Rather than handling requests on an ad-hoc basis with protracted processing times of up to a year, Supo should establish clear, legally anchored declassification timelines aligned with the Archives Act. When requests are made for academic or journalistic research, the default administrative posture should lean toward controlled access—such as redacted versions or secure reading room access—provided that personal data protections and legitimate national security thresholds are met. Granting qualified researchers structured access to the Tiitinen list would not only satisfy public interest and academic rigor but would also disarm lingering suspicions of institutional cover-ups, thereby strengthening the long-term credibility of Finland's security apparatus.

title: In the future, those who completed civil service can be ordered to refresher training and support duties in exceptional circumstances
originalSummary: Venäjän uhka ja puolustusministerin puheet aiheuttivat joukkopaon sotilasreservistä. Uusi laki mahdollistaisi eronneille paluun reserviin.
analysis:
The Finnish government is preparing major updates to the Civil Service Act of 2008 to align non-military service with Finland's updated security environment and comprehensive security model. Under the proposed legislation, civil service training will increase its emphasis on emergency preparedness, civil defense, and safety skills—such as oil spill control, missing person searches, and food supply management. The initial training period will be expanded from four to five weeks. Crucially, during exceptional circumstances like heightened military readiness, major accidents, or pandemics, individuals who have completed civil service can be ordered to take part in up to 40 days of mandatory refresher training and assigned to support civil authorities. The reform also addresses service flexibility: civil service participants will be allowed to switch to military service within their first week, and individuals who previously resigned from the military reserve to join civil service will be given a one-time option to return to the military reserve.

Modernizing the civil service framework enhances overall societal resilience by transforming a non-military service option into a practical component of national crisis preparedness. Historically, civil service in Finland has lacked a structured integration into broader emergency response mechanisms, often serving primarily as a labor substitute in civilian institutions rather than a targeted crisis reserve. Equipping civil servants with standardized safety and civil protection skillsets directly strengthens public capacity during non-military crises, hybrid threats, and natural disasters. Furthermore, permitting former soldiers who transferred to civil service to return to the military reserve rectifies an unnecessary rigid barrier in manpower allocation, allowing trained military personnel to re-enter primary defense structures if their personal views evolve.

From a policy perspective, this legislative reform should be pursued and implemented as planned, as it bridges the longstanding gap between non-military service and civil preparedness without undermining the constitutional right to conscientious objection. To maximize the utility of the reform, the curriculum during the expanded training weeks must be strictly aligned with operational emergency services, ensuring that skills acquired lead to actionable certifications in rescue operations and logistics. Additionally, the option to transition between military and non-military reserves should be permanently preserved as a flexible workforce management mechanism, ensuring the state maintains an accurate and willing defense inventory across both military and civil sectors.

title: Adlercreutz on Peltokangas's writing: 'Extremely inappropriate'
originalSummary: Kokoomus ja RKP vaativat asian käsittelyä perussuomalaisten eduskuntaryhmässä.
analysis:
Minister of Education Anders Adlercreutz (RKP) strongly criticized a social media post by Member of Parliament Mauri Peltokangas (PS) during an appearance on Yle's A-studio. Peltokangas had written on Facebook that the Social Democrats would provide their followers with 'their very own quota Muslim as a minister' if they win the upcoming elections. The post drew harsh criticism from government coalition partners, with Adlercreutz labeling the remarks extremely racist, inappropriate, and foolish, arguing that they rely on fear-mongering, stigmatization, and derogatory labeling. In response, the National Coalition Party and the Swedish People's Party (RKP) demanded that the Finns Party parliamentary group address the matter internally. However, Finns Party group leader Jani Mäkelä has not committed to initiating such a review, leading Adlercreutz to warn that if the party fails to handle the issue internally, it will be escalated to the parliamentary group leaders, with pre-agreed consequences already established between the National Coalition Party and RKP.

Political discourse utilizing ethnic or religious generalizations in democratic institutions undermines social cohesion and erodes trust in public administration. From a political science perspective, normalizing derogatory rhetoric against minority groups creates exclusionary barriers that hinder effective minority integration and public service delivery. When elected officials resort to identity-based stereotyping, it degrades the quality of legislative debate and distracts from substantive policy issues such as economic reform, education, and healthcare. Maintaining normative standards of civility is crucial for upholding institutional legitimacy and ensuring that governance remains focused on competence rather than polarizing identity politics.

To address this systemic issue constructively, coalition leadership must enforce strict ethical codes of conduct with tangible accountability mechanisms for inflammatory rhetoric. Merely shifting disputes between parliamentary group leaders often results in political theater rather than genuine behavioral change. Instead, political parties across the spectrum should establish transparent, binding disciplinary procedures for hate speech and targeted harassment to protect the integrity of public debate. Addressing such incidents firmly reinforces the principle that democratic representation requires upholding the dignity of all residents, thereby fostering a more stable and inclusive political environment necessary for effective policymaking.

title: Legendary Helkama Struggles with Millions in Losses – CEO: 'We Are Here to Stay'
originalSummary: Kotimaiset polkupyöräyritykset ovat vaikeuksissa. Helkama Velox uskoo tulevaisuuteen, korostaa toimitusjohtaja Tero Valtonen.
analysis:
The article reports on the severe financial distress facing historic Finnish bicycle manufacturers, focusing on Helkama Velox, whose factory in Hanko has temporarily halted production and laid off around 30 employees due to multi-million euro losses. While global post-pandemic oversupply and general consumer caution have created widespread industry headwinds, the company highlights a major domestic shock: the Finnish government's decision to eliminate the tax exemption for company bicycles. Because electric bicycles represent three-quarters of Helkama's revenue, the sudden abolition of this tax benefit created a sharp, ongoing drop in consumer and corporate demand, compounding existing macroeconomic struggles.

Evaluating the removal of the tax benefit for company bikes requires balancing fiscal discipline against broader public policy objectives such as public health, transport decarbonization, and market predictability. Fringe-benefit tax incentives for bicycles were designed to encourage active commuting and reduce urban transport emissions, serving as a relatively low-cost mechanism to shift commuting habits toward sustainable alternatives. Abruptly ending such a program introduces significant policy volatility, punishing businesses that made capital investments and long-term strategic pivots based on state-encouraged growth sectors. While tax expenditures must be periodically reviewed to prevent deadweight loss, unexpected and immediate policy shifts risk disproportionately damaging local industries and undermining public trust in government incentives.

To manage green transition policies and fiscal targets effectively, the government should prioritize regulatory stability and predictable implementation timelines rather than abrupt policy reversals. Sudden tax shifts generate artificial demand shocks that harm domestic supply chains and business confidence. Moving forward, changes to transport fringe-benefit taxation or environmental incentive schemes should incorporate adequate transition periods and clear impact assessments. Restoring clarity and consistency to sustainable transport frameworks will allow businesses to plan long-term investments while ensuring that public policy reliably supports active health and environmental targets.

title: Agriculture and Forestry Committee Holds Meeting on African Swine Fever
analysis:
The Finnish Parliament's Agriculture and Forestry Committee is convening to address the serious threat posed by the spread of African Swine Fever (ASF). Committee Chair Ritva Elomaa stated that the committee seeks up-to-date information on the evolving situation. To evaluate the risks and potential response measures, the committee plans to hear expert testimony from both the Finnish Food Authority (Ruokavirasto) and the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry.

From a policy perspective, proactive parliamentary oversight and expert consultations regarding infectious animal diseases are vital for protecting domestic agriculture and national food security. African Swine Fever is a highly contagious viral disease affecting domestic and wild pigs, carrying devastating economic consequences for swine farming and meat exports. Given the absence of a widely available vaccine, prevention relies almost entirely on strict biosecurity protocols, population management of wild boars, and rapid containment mechanisms. Parliamentary engagement ensures that regulatory bodies and ministries receive appropriate resources and legal backing to implement stringent preventive measures before an outbreak occurs within national borders.

To effectively safeguard the agricultural sector, policy responses should focus on reinforcing biosecurity standards across swine production facilities and enhancing monitoring of wild boar vectors along border regions. Authorities must maintain clear, rapid-response communication channels with farm operators, ensuring that biosecurity guidelines are rigorously enforced. Furthermore, coordination between the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry, border control authorities, and local veterinary services should be optimized to facilitate early detection and swift quarantine procedures, thereby minimizing systemic economic damage to the food supply chain.

title: Registration for the Sámi Parliament electoral roll underway – young people especially encouraged to apply
originalSummary: Suomen saamelaisnuorten yhdistys auttaa nuoria saamaan tietoa vaaliluetteloon hakemisesta. Puheenjohtajan mukaan nuorten on tärkeää osallistua vaaleihin.
analysis:
Registration for the upcoming Sámi Parliament elections in Finland is currently open, following a significant legislative reform of the Sámi Parliament Act. The revised law updated electoral eligibility criteria, most notably extending the language criterion to the fourth generation. Youth representatives and Sámi Parliament officials are actively urging eligible individuals—particularly young people and those not previously registered—to submit their applications before the end of September. Current voters who were registered in 2024 and continue to meet the requirements do not need to reapply. The application process requires submitting proof of eligibility, such as church registers or population certificates. Additionally, the reform extends the voting duration by two weeks, with the next elections scheduled for late summer and autumn of 2027.

From a policy perspective, updating the Sámi Parliament Act and broadening the electoral criteria is a necessary step toward aligning Finnish domestic law with international human rights standards regarding indigenous self-determination. The previous framework faced criticism from United Nations bodies for failing to respect the autonomy of the Sámi people in determining their own membership. Extending the language criterion acknowledges historical policies of assimilation and language loss, providing a fair legal pathway for descendants of Sámi speakers to reclaim their civic rights within the indigenous governance framework. Ensuring high electoral participation, especially among youth, is essential for maintaining the institutional legitimacy and democratic vitality of the parliament.

To maximize the positive policy impact of these legislative changes, administrative efficiency and accessible communication must be prioritized. The registration procedure relies heavily on applicants procuring historical population records, which creates unnecessary bureaucratic friction for young people. The Ministry of Justice and the Sámi Parliament Election Board should collaborate with the Digital and Population Data Services Agency to streamline document verification through digital inter-agency cooperation. Reducing administrative hurdles and providing transparent guidance will ensure that the expanded legal criteria translate effectively into broad democratic engagement without subjecting applicants to prolonged procedural uncertainty.

title: SDP's Nasima Razmyar on Finns Party Peltokangas's Muslim Post: 'Of course he is referring to me'
originalSummary: SDP:n kansanedustaja Nasima Razmyar pitää Mauri Peltokankaan kirjoitusta ”umpirasistisena”.
analysis:
Social Democratic Party (SDP) MP and First Vice Chair Nasima Razmyar responded to a social media post by Finns Party MP Mauri Peltokangas, who wrote that the SDP would appoint a 'quota Muslim minister' if they win the next election and questioned whether a Muslim politician would represent the interests of native Finns. Razmyar identified the remarks as targeting her and characterized them as outright racism. Peltokangas serves as the Chairman of the Administration Committee in the Finnish Parliament. The incident drew reactions across political lines, with the Swedish People's Party (RKP) parliamentary group leader calling the comments racist, the National Coalition Party (Kokoomus) demanding the Finns Party address the matter internally, and SDP Chair Antti Lindtman calling on Prime Minister Petteri Orpo to intervene, questioning whether the government's stated zero-tolerance policy on racism is being upheld.

From a governance and political institutional perspective, public discourse and official conduct by senior parliamentary figures—such as committee chairs—directly influence democratic norms, institutional trust, and social cohesion. Rhetoric that targets individuals based on religion or ethnic background creates friction within legislative bodies and undermines democratic representation by questioning the legitimacy of elected officials based on their personal identity rather than their political platform. Maintaining robust standards of conduct for parliamentary leadership is necessary to ensure that legislative committees operate with institutional credibility, as these bodies oversee critical domestic policy, legislative drafting, and public administration.

To address recurring disputes surrounding political rhetoric and uphold non-discrimination standards, parliamentary institutions should enforce clear, enforceable codes of conduct for committee leadership and high-ranking MPs. When committee chairs engage in conduct that directly conflicts with fundamental non-discrimination principles, political parties and parliamentary groups must implement structured accountability mechanisms rather than relying on informal group processing. Ensuring that all elected representatives are held to uniform standards of professional conduct strengthens legislative integrity, reduces polarization, and reinforces the constitutional principle that all citizens and elected officials participate equally in the democratic process regardless of background.

title: True Finns Jani Mäkelä takes no stance on whether Peltokangas's speech will be scrutinized: "It remains to be seen"
originalSummary: Hallituskumppani kokoomuksen eduskuntaryhmän puheenjohtaja Jukka Kopra pitää kirjoitusta asiattomana. Peltokangas kirjoitti muun muassa ”kiintiömuslimista”.
analysis:
The article details a political controversy surrounding a Facebook post by Finns Party Member of Parliament Mauri Peltokangas, in which he wrote that Social Democrats would provide a "quota Muslim as minister" if they win elections, questioning whether such a figure would represent native Finns. Jani Mäkelä, the chair of the Finns Party parliamentary group, downplayed the need for immediate internal disciplinary action, stating that the matter would be addressed in due course when parliament reconvenes. However, the statement drew sharp criticism from coalition partner National Coalition Party (Kokoomus), with MP Jukka Kopra labeling the comments inappropriate and calling for the Finns Party leadership to assess the situation against the government's anti-racism guidelines established last autumn. Other high-ranking Kokoomus ministers, such as Antti Häkkänen and Sari Multala, also criticized the personal nature of the criticism, while opposition SDP leader Antti Lindtman demanded Prime Minister Petteri Orpo intervene, arguing the post was a direct attack against SDP politician Nasima Razmyar. Peltokangas denied targeting Razmyar, and Mäkelä defended the core question as a legitimate topic of political discourse regarding the selection of political representatives.

This incident highlights the ongoing friction within the Finnish coalition government regarding political rhetoric and the practical implementation of ethical guidelines agreed upon to curb hate speech and discrimination. The establishment of specific anti-racism communication rules by the government was intended to signal a zero-tolerance approach toward derogatory statements targeting minorities or specific individuals based on background. However, the ambiguity in enforcement and the reluctance of party leadership to swiftly penalize members who test these boundaries undermine the credibility of such policy instruments. When coalition partners publicly clash over statements made by MPs, it exposes the fragility of agreed-upon normative frameworks designed to maintain civil discourse and institutional standards within the cabinet.

From a governance perspective, the enforcement mechanisms regarding anti-racism guidelines must be applied consistently and transparently to maintain public trust in administrative and legislative integrity. Allowing prolonged internal reviews without clear accountability weakens the deterrent effect of agreed-upon codes of conduct. The Finns Party leadership should explicitly clarify the boundaries of acceptable political discourse, ensuring that debates about political representation focus on substantive policy platforms and governance competencies rather than identity-based generalizations. Concurrently, coalition partners must hold each other accountable through established institutional mechanisms rather than public social media disputes, ensuring that adherence to common ethical standards remains a pillar of governmental stability and democratic norms.

title: Initiative Demanding Dismissal of Committee Chair Advances to Akaa Council – He Does Not Intend to Resign Voluntarily
originalSummary: 11 akaalaisvaltuutettua vaatii Anton Murolan (ps.) erottamista tarkastuslautakunnan puheenjohtajan tehtävästä rasististen somekirjoitusten vuoksi.
analysis:
The city board of Akaa has voted to submit a proposal to the city council to set up a temporary committee tasked with preparing the dismissal of the leadership of the city's audit committee. This decision follows an initiative signed by eleven local councillors demanding the removal of Anton Murola, a member of the Finns Party, from his role as chair of the audit committee after he repeatedly posted racist and derogatory comments about immigrants on social media. Under Finnish municipal law, a city council has the legal authority to dismiss the leadership of a municipal body before the end of their term if they no longer enjoy the council's trust. Murola has stated that he will not resign voluntarily, maintaining that his personal social media activity is entirely separate from his official role as an elected official and that he has committed no administrative errors in office. While the local Finns Party parliamentary group supports Murola, the city administration has reinforced its commitment to equal treatment and human dignity.

From a public administration and political perspective, the integrity and reputation of municipal institutions depend heavily on the public trust invested in their leaders. Audit committees, in particular, hold a vital oversight role in local governance, requiring a high standard of objectivity, credibility, and adherence to legal and ethical norms. Public officials who engage in hate speech or dehumanizing language undermine the foundational democratic principles of non-discrimination and equality enshrined in Finnish law. From an institutional viewpoint, separating a politician's public mandate from their public statements on open platforms is unviable, as public trust is holistic. Allowing individuals in key supervisory roles to retain office while expressing discriminatory views risks degrading citizen trust in public institutions and can impair the functional efficiency of municipal administration.

To safeguard institutional integrity, local councils should decisively utilize the administrative procedures provided by the Municipal Act when public trust has been compromised. Rather than relying on voluntary resignations, local governance bodies must demonstrate that ethical boundaries and statutory principles of equality are actively enforced. The creation of a temporary committee provides a structured, legally sound, and transparent mechanism to assess whether the loss of trust justifies formal dismissal, ensuring due process while upholding democratic accountability. Municipalities should also strengthen local codes of conduct and ethical frameworks to clearly signal that positions of public trust carry inherent responsibilities regarding public discourse and non-discrimination.

title: A Family in East Helsinki Opted into a School Many Avoid – 'The Discussion Has Had a Racist Undertone'
originalSummary: Helsingin kaupungin päätös muuttaa koulupiirirajoja on herättänyt kiivasta keskustelua muun muassa koulushoppailusta.
analysis:
The article details the public debate surrounding the redrawing of primary school catchment areas in Eastern Helsinki, a policy decision taken by the municipal education committee to redistribute student capacity and curb socio-ethnic school segregation. Under the new boundaries, children from neighborhoods such as Herttoniemi and Myllypuro will gradually be assigned to Itäkeskus Primary School, where 65 percent of pupils—and 84 percent of first-graders—currently speak Finnish as a second language (S2). While some local parents praise the school's broad language offerings and positive learning environment, criticizing public skepticism as biased, affected parents in Herttoniemi have mounted formal legal appeals. Their primary objections center on significantly longer and riskier walking routes across busy roads, alongside concerns about language support needs in high-S2 classrooms. Urban researchers noted in the article emphasize that parent mobility away from diverse areas is predominantly driven by public order and safety concerns rather than low trust in local schools.

From an educational and municipal policy standpoint, using administrative redistricting to balance school enrollment and prevent socio-spatial segregation is a recognized governance tool. Educational equity research demonstrates that extreme concentration of language support needs can stretch teaching resources and exacerbate disparities in educational attainment across neighborhoods. However, relying on boundary redrawing as a primary solution often proves inefficient when it runs counter to parental preferences and urban geography. Forcing young children onto longer and more perilous commute paths imposes real operational burdens on households, which risks triggering unintended consequences such as increased school shopping, flight to private or specialized schools, or residential mobility out of the district. Furthermore, boundary shifts treat the symptoms of neighborhood segregation rather than the structural drivers, such as housing policy, concentrated social housing, and localized public order issues.

To manage public education effectively, municipal decision-makers should refine their approach by prioritizing voluntary incentives and holistic urban planning over rigid administrative redistricting. Cities should focus on enhancing the intrinsic attraction of schools in socio-economically diverse areas through targeted financial weighting, reduced class sizes, specialized language immersion programs, or focused academic tracks. This incentivizes organic integration without burdening young students with longer commutes. Additionally, municipal authorities must coordinate education policy with housing and public safety measures to address the environmental factors—such as public substance use and safety perceptions—that drive residential flight. When catchment area adjustments are strictly necessary due to school building capacities, they must be paired with safe transit infrastructure improvements and introduced with proactive community dialogue to preserve public trust in the local school system.

title: Schools Start Today Across Most of the Country: Here Is How Daily Life Changes
originalSummary: Viime vuonna käyttöön otettu kännykkäkielto on ollut kouluarkeen kaivattu uudistus. Nyt osa kouluista kaavailee tiukentavansa sitä.
analysis:
As schools reopen across Finland for the new academic year, students and educators face significant operational changes driven by recent national policy and legislative updates. Following the introduction of a law restricting mobile phone use during lessons a year ago, a new statutory obligation now mandates that early childhood and basic education providers actively promote a physically active lifestyle among students. According to Terhi Nissinen, Head of Unit at the Finnish National Agency for Education, this requirement will fundamentally alter school routines. Lesson planning will increasingly prioritize physical activity, movement breaks, and playful learning methods, while recess times will incorporate structured games, peer-led activities, and enhanced play equipment. Furthermore, local education providers are actively updating their institutional rules to extend mobile phone bans beyond classroom hours to cover recesses, lunch breaks, and passing periods, following national guidelines.

Addressing youth physical inactivity and smartphone-induced distraction within the public school system directly targets critical public health and educational challenges. Scientific evidence consistently demonstrates that regular physical movement improves executive function, memory retention, and mental well-being in children, while excessive screen time and constant digital notifications impair concentration, lower academic performance, and impede real-world social interaction. Leveraging the universal public school system ensures that health interventions reach all children regardless of socio-economic background, making it an efficient vehicle for population-level health promotion. However, introducing broad statutory mandates risks placing additional administrative and supervisory burdens on teaching staff without guaranteeing consistent execution. If schools lack adequate physical infrastructure, equipment, or teacher training, the policy may result in superficial compliance rather than genuine behavioral change.

To ensure these statutory objectives yield long-term positive outcomes, policy implementation should focus on national standardization and structural support. Rather than relying on individual municipal education providers to independently update local rules, the government should establish a uniform nationwide policy prohibiting non-pedagogical smartphone use throughout the entire school day, including recesses and lunchtimes. This would eliminate enforcement ambiguity and ensure an equal learning environment across all municipalities. Additionally, the promotion of physical activity must be backed by dedicated pedagogical resources, physical equipment grants, and standardized best-practice toolkits for teachers. By combining clear digital boundaries with properly funded opportunities for daily physical movement, Finland can protect academic focus while effectively improving youth health outcomes.

title: Etla Study: Tax Increases Should Not Be Implemented – 'Extremely Negative Impact on the Economy'
originalSummary: Tutkimuksen mukaan julkista taloutta tulisi tasapainottaa mieluummin menosopeutuksilla kuin veronkorotuksilla.
analysis:
A new study by the Research Institute of the Finnish Economy (Etla) argues that Finland's upcoming fiscal consolidation should focus primarily on spending cuts rather than tax increases. According to University of Helsinki docent Juha Tervala, one of the report's authors, fiscal multipliers in Finland are particularly high for tax increases, meaning that raising taxes inflicts greater damage on gross domestic product than cutting public spending. This dynamic is exacerbated by Finland's membership in the eurozone, which precludes independent monetary easing, and its already high overall tax burden. The report warns that attempting to achieve the required 8 to 11 billion euro fiscal adjustment solely through tax hikes would impose an untenable burden on middle-class wage earners and retirees, severely depressing private consumption. While spending cuts also reduce economic output and employment—especially if targeted at public investment or government payrolls—the study suggests that targeted reductions in public expenditure, including transfer payments, represent the less damaging route. Finns Party leader Riikka Purra noted in response that balancing the budget without tax hikes is difficult but achievable.

The findings align with established macroeconomic literature on fiscal consolidations, which demonstrates that expenditure-based adjustments are generally less harmful to long-term growth and more successful at reducing debt-to-GDP ratios than revenue-based adjustments. In a country like Finland, where high marginal tax rates already create distortions in labor supply, consumption, and investment decisions, further tax hikes push economic actors further along the Laffer curve, compounding efficiency losses. When consumption taxes like VAT are raised, immediate contractionary pressures hit domestic demand and reduce the purchasing power of households. Conversely, while public spending cuts temporarily dampen aggregate demand, they do not introduce permanent microeconomic distortions into work incentives or business capital allocation to the same degree as tax increases.

To navigate the required fiscal consolidation with minimal economic drag, policymakers should strictly adhere to an expenditure-led strategy while carefully selectively shielding high-multiplier spending categories. Specifically, public investment in infrastructure and essential growth-enhancing capital, as well as core public sector operational capacity, should be insulated from blanket cuts, as reducing these areas yields severe negative spillovers into private sector productivity. Instead, expenditure reductions must be focused on streamlining statutory social transfer payments and non-core subsidization programs. Tax increases should be explicitly ruled out as a primary consolidation mechanism, as raising the tax burden in an already high-tax regime would stagnate medium-term GDP growth and ultimately undermine the very tax base required to stabilize public finances.

title: Finns Party's Mauri Peltokangas asked about "Muslim-Demrats" on Facebook – Lindtman demands action from Orpo
originalSummary: SDP:n puheenjohtaja Antti Lindtman totesi Mauri Peltokankaan (ps.) kirjoituksen olleen suora hyökkäys Nasima Razmyaria (sd.) kohtaan. Peltokangas kiistää kirjoittaneensa Razmyarista.
analysis:
Social Democratic Party (SDP) chair Antti Lindtman has called on Prime Minister Petteri Orpo to address social media comments made by Finns Party MP Mauri Peltokangas. Peltokangas posted on Facebook suggesting that the SDP would install a "quota Muslim minister" if they win power, questioning whether such a figure would represent the interests of native Finns, and asking his followers how many would want an Afghan-Muslim serving as Minister of the Interior or Foreign Affairs. Lindtman argued the post was a direct and unacceptable attack against SDP MP Nasima Razmyar, who was born in Afghanistan and is openly Muslim. While Peltokangas claimed the term was merely a figure of speech referring to future demographic representation within political parties and denied targeting Razmyar specifically, the comments drew widespread criticism from other coalition figures, including Kokoomus (National Coalition Party) MPs Jukka Kopra, Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen, and Environment and Climate Minister Sari Multala, who called on the Finns Party leadership to intervene.

From a governance and political ethics perspective, public discourse targeting politicians based on their ethnic or religious background undermines the foundational principles of representative democracy. In modern parliamentary systems, legislators are elected to represent constituencies based on their political platforms, competence, and policy stances rather than their ethnic origins or religious affiliations. Rhetoric that frames minority politicians through a lens of suspicion or as foreign elements poses systemic risks to social cohesion and civic trust. Research in political science consistently demonstrates that inclusive political representation enhances institutional legitimacy and fosters greater civic engagement among diverse populations. Conversely, political messaging that Otherizes minority politicians can chill participation, degrade the quality of public debate, and normalize xenophobic tropes within mainstream political discourse, ultimately impairing the efficiency of governance by diverting attention away from substantive legislative and economic challenges.

Addressing this situation requires a clear reaffirmation of democratic norms and institutional boundaries by political leadership. Prime Minister Petteri Orpo and the leadership of the governing coalition must draw a firm line against rhetoric that questions the legitimacy of duly elected representatives based on identity rather than policy. While freedom of speech protects robust political debate, elected officials bear a heightened responsibility to maintain a standard of decorum that respects the equality of all citizens and parliamentarians. Rather than allowing such rhetoric to distract from critical national policy issues, the government should formally distance itself from identity-based attacks and prioritize legislative agendas that unite the electorate around shared socioeconomic goals. Enforcing internal party accountability and upholding parliamentary standards are essential steps to ensure that political competition remains focused on policy efficacy rather than polarizing identity politics.

title: Economic Forecasters Defend Against Criticism – Ministry of Finance Director General: 'Decimals As Such Are Not Important, the Story Is'
originalSummary: Kalevi Sorsa -säätiö arvostelee poliittisten päätösten pohjana olevia talousennusteita epätarkkuudesta. Ennustajat syyttävät kriitikoita shokkien unohtamisesta.
analysis:
A critical report published by the Kalevi Sorsa Foundation has sparked debate over the reliability of economic forecasts and their role in guiding political decision-making in Finland. Researchers from the foundation questioned using macroeconomic projections as the primary foundation for state budget planning, pointing out significant forecasting errors across major institutions, including the Ministry of Finance, the Bank of Finland, and research institutes such as Etla, PTT, Labore, OP, and Nordea. In response, Mikko Spolander, Director General at the Ministry of Finance, along with other economic analysts, defended the utility of forecasts. They highlighted that recent years have seen unprecedented global shocks—such as the COVID-19 pandemic, Russia's invasion of Ukraine, soaring inflation, and rapid interest rate hikes—making accurate predictions exceptionally difficult. Furthermore, forecasters rely heavily on preliminary data from Statistics Finland, which is frequently subject to major retroactive revisions. Spolander argued that the primary value of macroeconomic forecasts lies not in precise decimal projections, but in providing a coherent, internally consistent narrative of the economy to guide leaders, rejecting proposals to substitute macroeconomic models with isolated real-time indicators like monthly tax revenues.

Evaluating the role of macroeconomic forecasting in fiscal policy underscores a fundamental tension between long-term strategic coherence and short-term operational responsiveness. Macroeconomic models serve a critical function in public policy by tying together disparate economic sectors—such as household consumption, business investment, trade balances, and labor dynamics—into a unified framework. Without such models, budget planning risks becoming reactive and fragmented. However, over-relying on point-estimate growth forecasts to justify rigid fiscal policy rules or spending caps creates significant systemic vulnerabilities. When initial GDP figures understate actual growth by nearly a full percentage point, as occurred recently in Finland, fiscal policy risks becoming unnecessarily pro-cyclical, inadvertently suppressing economic activity through premature austerity measures based on false premises.

To improve fiscal policy formulation, the decision-making framework should evolve beyond single point-estimate forecasting toward probabilistic, scenario-based budgeting. The Ministry of Finance and political leaders should refrain from anchoring rigid budget targets to specific decimal projections of GDP growth. Instead, fiscal planning should systematically incorporate sensitivity analyses and ranges that account for statistical margins of error and revision lags. Simultaneously, while macroeconomic models must remain central to medium-term fiscal strategy, incorporating high-frequency, real-time indicators—such as monthly tax collection data and employment rolls—can serve as valuable early-warning mechanisms to test model assumptions continuously. Bridging structural macroeconomic modeling with real-time data integration will create a more resilient policy framework capable of adapting to economic volatility without abandoning systemic foresight.

title: Finnwatch Resigns from Advisory Board on Corporate Responsibility – 'Massimuijat' Case Was the Final Straw
originalSummary: Yhteiskunta- ja yritysvastuun neuvottelukunnan puheenjohtaja pitää Finnwatchin lähtöä valitettavana.
analysis:
The non-governmental organization Finnwatch has announced its resignation from the Advisory Board on Corporate Social Responsibility, an advisory entity operating under the Finnish Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment. Finnwatch cited long-standing operational problems and concluded that the board in its current form is unable to perform its statutory and advisory functions effectively. The final catalyst for the departure was the handling of the so-called 'massimuijat' case, in which social media influencer Natalia Salmela and audit firm KPMG marketed legal tax avoidance strategies to influencers. The advisory board determined that KPMG had not breached the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises on Responsible Business Conduct. Jan Hjelt, the board's chairman and a department head at the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment, expressed regret over the resignation, noting that discussions had been scheduled for the autumn to evaluate the board's future role, operational constraints, and potential procedural or regulatory reforms, though any legislative changes would fall to the next parliamentary term. Finnwatch's Executive Director Sonja Finér criticized the board for setting an unreasonably high burden of proof for complainants, highlighting that the advisory board has not issued a single non-compliance finding in its nearly 18 years of operation.

The resignation of Finnwatch underscores structural weaknesses in how soft-law oversight and corporate responsibility frameworks are implemented in Finland. Advisory bodies that act as OECD National Contact Points require operational legitimacy, clear mandates, and effective procedural mechanisms to fulfill their mandate of encouraging responsible business conduct. When an oversight entity fails to issue a single adverse finding in nearly two decades while placing a heavy evidentiary burden on civil society actors, its institutional utility as a fair mediator or watchdog becomes severely diminished. Soft-law instruments rely on public credibility and transparency; without robust fact-finding capabilities or an equitable dispute resolution process, such bodies risk acting as mere institutional covers that legitimize questionable corporate practices rather than curbing them. Furthermore, as tax responsibility and corporate governance become increasingly integrated into broader economic stability, the lack of effective state-backed oversight mechanisms damages public trust in systemic fairness.

To address this regulatory deficit, the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment should overhaul the Advisory Board on Corporate Social Responsibility rather than maintaining an ambiguous governance structure. The ministry ought to explicitly re-evaluate whether the board should function purely as a conciliation and dialogue forum—similar to models in other OECD countries—or be restructured into an independent supervisory body with formal statutory powers. If the board is retained as a decision-making entity, legislative reforms should be introduced to grant it adequate resources, independent fact-finding capabilities, and realistic evidentiary standards so that complainants are not unfairly disadvantaged. Additionally, in light of incoming European Union directives on corporate sustainability due diligence, Finland should proactively align its national oversight bodies with binding transparency standards, ensuring that corporate tax strategies and ethical guidelines are subject to genuine, accountable scrutiny.

title: Analysis: The electricity meter allows your home's electricity to be cut off remotely – who do you want to be able to do it?
originalSummary: Antaako viranomaisvalvonta ja tuottomahdollisuuksien rajaaminen riittävän otteen sähköverkkoyhtiöihin, kysyy taloustoimittaja Jarmo Koponen.
analysis:
The article examines the transfer of the majority ownership of Caruna, Finland's largest electricity network company, to a foreign owner, sparking a renewed debate over critical infrastructure control, transmission pricing, and national security. The author highlights consumer frustrations regarding rising transmission fees, which network companies justify through investment needs while simultaneously generating profits for owners. A central security concern raised is the remote disconnect capability embedded in modern smart electricity meters owned by these network companies, alongside the potential for new fees based on peak consumption data. The piece questions whether reactive regulatory oversight by public authorities is sufficient for critical infrastructure or if foreign ownership poses structural risks due to board-level access to sensitive data, vulnerability assessments, and ICT systems. Furthermore, it addresses the dilemma municipalities face when selling network assets for short-term financial relief versus retaining democratic control over regional monopolies in an era of decentralized energy production like solar panels and batteries.

From a regulatory and economic perspective, critical infrastructure such as electricity transmission networks operates as a natural monopoly, meaning market competition cannot naturally regulate prices or service quality. When these monopolies are privatized or sold to foreign entities, the profit motive inherently conflicts with consumer welfare, necessitating stringent ex-ante and ex-post regulation by public authorities. Economic research consistently shows that infrastructure privatization often leads to higher efficiency investments but frequently results in rent-extraction through consumer fees unless price caps and quality standards are meticulously enforced. Moreover, national security dimensions in critical infrastructure go beyond mere economic efficiency; foreign ownership of grid management systems introduces potential geopolitical vulnerabilities, supply chain risks, and concerns regarding state-sponsored cyber threats or operational interference, particularly given that modern smart grids rely heavily on interconnected digital infrastructure and remote-control capabilities.

To safeguard consumer interests and national security without stifling necessary infrastructure investments, the regulatory framework governing electricity distribution networks must be fundamentally tightened. Public authorities should shift from predominantly reactive oversight to proactive, continuous monitoring of network companies' operational decisions, cybersecurity protocols, and financial flows. Municipalities and the state should carefully weigh the long-term strategic value of retaining public control over regional monopolies rather than trading enduring infrastructure dividends for short-term budget relief. If private or foreign ownership is permitted, regulatory authorities must mandate stricter caps on allowable returns on capital, tie profit margins directly to measurable reliability and security standards, and restrict board-level access to sensitive national security data for foreign entities. Ultimately, because electricity is an indispensable public utility vital to societal functioning, democratic oversight and strategic state control over the physical grid and its remote-management architecture should be prioritized to ensure resilience, affordability, and public trust.

title: Controversial STEA Decree Reaches Government on Thursday, Meeting Deadline
originalSummary: Pääministeri Petteri Orpo asetti kesäkuussa työryhmän määrittämään asetuksella, millä perustein avustuksia jaetaan.
analysis:
The Finnish government is scheduled to present a revised decree regarding the criteria for distributing subsidies through the Funding Centre for Social Welfare and Health Organisations (STEA). This presentation follows months of disagreement within the cabinet, sparked by Minister of Social Affairs and Health Wille Rydman's implementation of stricter funding criteria for social and health non-governmental organizations (NGOs). In response to the rift, Prime Minister Petteri Orpo formed a task force of permanent secretaries to draft a decree intended to overturn the minister's restrictive additions. Although the draft has passed technical refinements and received ministerial permission for presentation, the Chancellor of Justice highlighted critical legal ambiguities, noting that the document fails to clarify whether a minister can legally bypass the decree and enforce individual criteria. The actual operational weight of the decree relative to ministerial discretion will ultimately be tested when grant decisions are executed early next year.

From a public policy and administrative governance perspective, the framework governing state subsidies to third-sector organizations must prioritize predictability, transparency, and objective criteria. Social and health NGOs perform vital complementary functions in preventive care, mental health support, and community assistance, often reducing burdens on the primary public healthcare system. When subsidy frameworks suffer from legal vagueness or allow for unpredictable political intervention, civil society organizations lose the stability required for multi-year operational planning. Furthermore, ambiguous regulations that leave room for ministerial overrides create unnecessary administrative friction, risk violating equal treatment principles under administrative law, and potentially lead to costly legal disputes.

To establish an efficient and sustainable framework for social sector funding, the government should ensure that the decree establishes definitive, legally binding criteria that eliminate arbitrary discretionary overrides by individual ministers. Policy changes regarding grant distribution should occur strictly through transparent regulatory processes accompanied by public consultation and thorough impact assessments. Additionally, the criteria for STEA allocations should be anchored in verifiable effectiveness and socio-economic utility metrics rather than political alignment, ensuring that public resources generate the highest possible social return while maintaining total legal clarity.

title: City Boards Decided: Vantaa and Espoo to Start City-Wide Co-determination Negotiations
originalSummary: Espoo tavoittelee säästöjä, vaikka kaupungin talous on ylijäämäinen. Vantaan talous on ollut alijäämäinen useampien vuosien ajan.
analysis:
The city boards of Vantaa and Espoo have decided to initiate city-wide co-determination negotiations aimed at reducing municipal personnel expenditures. Both municipalities have explicitly exempted teaching and pedagogical staff working in schools and daycares from these negotiations. In Vantaa, the goal is to achieve 15 million euros in savings through approximately 200 redundancies, alongside temporary layoffs and conversions to part-time roles, to tackle a severe structural deficit projected to exceed 60 million euros this year and nearly 70 million euros next year. In Espoo, the city aims to reduce up to 300 full-time equivalent positions to cut annual workforce costs by 10 million euros through layoffs, retirements, and voluntary internal transfers. Despite Espoo currently reporting a financial surplus, Mayor Kai Mykkänen defended the move as necessary to curb rising per-capita debt caused by major infrastructure investments—including building 20 schools and daycares and the local city rail project—as well as state-driven cuts to municipal central government transfers and corporate tax revenue shares.

From a public finance and administrative perspective, addressing municipal fiscal imbalances is necessary to ensure the long-term solvency of local governance. Protecting core educational and early childhood services is a rational decision, as human capital investments yield substantial long-term economic returns and societal stability. However, relying on broad labor negotiations in public administration often generates significant operational friction, reduces public sector productivity, and risks worsening service bottlenecks in non-exempted sectors. Espoo's situation highlights a structural challenge in municipal accounting: nominal fiscal surpluses do not guarantee adequate cash flow when capital expenditure requirements are elevated due to rapid population growth. Moreover, national decision-making that reduces municipal state transfers shifts central fiscal pressure directly onto municipal payrolls, exposing a fundamental mismatch between central government mandates and local financial autonomy.

To manage municipal finances sustainably without compromising public service quality, local leadership must shift from reactive head-count reductions toward structural modernization and administrative reform. Personnel savings should be realized primarily through voluntary turnover, retirement turnover, and aggressive digital automation of internal workflows rather than abrupt redundancies that create operational instability. Simultaneously, the central government must ensure fiscal coherence: when municipal state transfers are reduced, legislative requirements and administrative burdens placed on municipalities must be scaled back proportionally. For fast-growing cities undergoing major urban development, infrastructure projects should be phased strategically or financed through public-private risk-sharing mechanisms to prevent physical capital investments from overly squeezing operational workforce budgets.

title: Parents Must Limit Their Social Media Use, Says World-Renowned Finnish Researcher
originalSummary: Pasi Sahlberg on maailmalla ylistetty suomalainen kasvatustieteilijä. Hän sai vastattavakseen suuren kysymyksen: olemmeko jo menettäneet ikäluokkia somelle?
analysis:
Pasi Sahlberg, a prominent Finnish professor of education at the University of Melbourne, addresses the rising global concerns regarding youth mental health, declining learning outcomes, and reduced attention spans attributed to social media. While acknowledging the serious risks and harmful consequences of excessive screen time, Sahlberg cautions against simplistic, binary debate and top-down policy measures. Referencing OECD findings, he notes that moderate leisure time spent on digital devices—roughly one to three hours per day—is associated with better academic performance and higher school satisfaction than total abstention or excessive use, as digital media can strengthen friendships and support social well-being. Sahlberg strongly criticizes statutory bans, such as Australia's prohibition of social media for minors and similar policy discussions or school phone bans in Finland. He characterizes such legislative bans as politically driven measures aimed at securing adult votes that offer temporary relief like aspirin while ignoring young people's perspectives and failing to yield long-term educational benefits. Instead, Sahlberg advocates for a tripartite framework based on shared responsibility between schools, parents, and children. This model emphasizes teaching digital literacy rather than demonizing technology, encouraging parents to model healthy habits by reducing their own screen time, and establishing mutual family agreements regarding device usage.

From a policy perspective, relying on legislative bans to curb digital harm presents severe administrative challenges and limited efficacy. Statutory prohibitions on platform access or mobile devices are notoriously difficult to enforce, often driving online activity onto unmonitored channels or fostering circumvention rather than instilling responsible digital habits. Research demonstrates that blanket bans in educational settings do not automatically guarantee improved learning outcomes or a reduction in bullying, primarily because they fail to address the underlying behavioral and environmental drivers of overuse, such as lack of physical activity, poor sleep hygiene, and insufficient real-world recreational opportunities. Regulatory interventions that rely on outright prohibition treat digital tools as inherently harmful, missing the nuanced reality that digital connectivity plays a legitimate role in modern adolescent socialization and identity formation. Furthermore, top-down state mandates risk placing an undue enforcement burden on educators while disempowering parents and youth from developing self-regulatory competence.

Policymakers should move away from high-profile statutory bans and direct state efforts toward regulatory framework design, digital pedagogy, and public health support. Government action should prioritize forcing social media companies to reform addictive algorithmic feeds, enforce strict default privacy settings for minors, and curb predatory engagement tactics through robust digital service regulation. Domestically, education policy should focus on integrating comprehensive digital media literacy into school curricula, helping students understand algorithmic incentives and cognitive self-regulation rather than imposing simple bans. State resources should be directed toward expanding accessible offline youth services, physical sports, and community spaces to ensure attractive alternatives to screen time exist. Ultimately, policy should support schools and parents in establishing localized, collaborative digital boundaries rather than substituting family and educational responsibility with heavy-handed statutory prohibitions.

title: Expert: Highly Educated Parents Engage in School Shopping, and in Some Areas 'It Can Look Like Racism'
originalSummary: Koulujen valikointi keskittyy etenkin alueille, joissa asuu paljon vieraskielisiä. Valikointia tekevät eniten korkeasti koulutettujen lasten vanhemmat.
analysis:
Recent changes to school intake boundaries in East Helsinki have sparked a broader debate on school selection, commonly known as school shopping, and socio-spatial segregation in Finnish municipalities. According to Annette Ukkola, a leading evaluation expert at the Finnish National Centre for Education Evaluation (Karvi), highly educated parents frequently select primary and secondary schools based on perceived quality, often avoiding institutions located in socioeconomically disadvantaged areas with high proportions of foreign-language (S2) students. This selection frequently occurs through specialized learning tracks introduced in the third and seventh grades. Ukkola highlights that empirical evidence does not support the belief that attending a supposedly superior school significantly enhances an individual student's learning outcomes, as parental educational background remains the primary determinant of academic success. Furthermore, high-performing students achieve strong results regardless of the average competence level in their classroom. However, school shopping concentrates privileged students into specific tracks and schools, leaving neighborhood schools with higher proportions of non-native speakers, which can foster perceptions of ethnic avoidance. While Finland still maintains high baseline equality compared to international standards—with 93 percent of first-graders entering their local municipal school—reputational stigmatization and shifting demographics pose a growing challenge to educational equity.

From a policy perspective, school shopping presents a classic structural conflict between parental autonomy and social cohesion. Unchecked school choice accelerates educational segregation, creating a self-reinforcing cycle where neighborhood schools in lower-income areas suffer from declining public perception, reduced peer-group benefits, and disproportionate administrative burdens, regardless of actual teaching quality. Specialized tracks (painotettu opetus), while designed to foster talent and motivation, function as a soft tracking system that socioeconomically privileged families navigate far more effectively. While Finland attempts to counteract these imbalances through state equality funding directed at disadvantaged districts, resource allocation alone is insufficient to dismantle persistent social stigmas or neutralize peer-effect dynamics. Allowing structural segregation to deepen threatens the long-term sustainability of the Finnish comprehensive school model, which relies on high-quality, socioeconomically integrated local schools to ensure societal mobility.

To preserve educational equity and mitigate school shopping, policymakers and municipal authorities must reform the structural drivers of segregation rather than relying solely on post-hoc financial compensation. First, municipalities should re-evaluate early specialized tracking mechanisms, integrating talent development and enrichment directly into mainstream classrooms instead of creating separate, stratified cohorts within schools. Second, local authorities must use smart, balanced catchment area planning that deliberately combines socioeconomically diverse residential zones into unified intake districts, preventing the formation of isolated high-poverty schools. Finally, municipal education departments should actively publish transparent, objective data on school resources, teacher qualifications, and learning support to dispel unfounded local rumors and reputational biases. Paired with intensive early Finnish-language immersion programs to ensure non-native students quickly achieve academic fluency, these structural measures will restore confidence in local comprehensive schools and ensure equal educational opportunities across all neighborhood boundaries.

title: Report: Economic Forecasts Mostly Go Badly Wrong, Yet Decisions Are Made Based on Them
originalSummary: Ennusteet talouskasvusta menevät tavallisesti metsään ja paljon, kertoo Kalevi Sorsa -säätiö. Poliittisia päätöksiä tehdään silti niiden perusteella.
analysis:
A recent report published by the Kalevi Sorsa Foundation, a Finnish Social Democratic think tank, strongly criticizes the tight coupling between macroeconomic forecasts and political decision-making in Finland. Authors Lauri Finér and Jussi Systä analyzed economic growth predictions from seven major institutions, including the Ministry of Finance, the Bank of Finland, research institutes, and major commercial banks, between 2016 and 2025. The study concludes that forecasters rarely predict economic turning points or next-year growth accurately, with autumn GDP growth estimates for the following year missing the actual outcome by an average of one percentage point. The problem is amplified by the preliminary statistical data provided by Statistics Finland, which forms the baseline for these models; preliminary estimates themselves deviate from final verified figures by an average of 0.7 percentage points. Despite these structural inaccuracies, major policy choices—including the government's annual budget allocations, long-term strategic plans, and statutory spending cuts dictated by the national debt brake framework—are legally or procedurally tied to these projections. The report warns that systematically over- or underestimating growth risks driving counterproductive fiscal policies, such as excessive austerity that further harms economic growth. Consequently, the authors advise against binding policy choices tightly to fixed forecast numbers, suggesting instead dynamic policy adjustments based on confirmed economic indicators, greater use of real-time metrics like monthly employment and tax revenues, and improved transparency in forecasting methodologies.

From a policy perspective, relying on quantitative economic forecasts to anchor government spending and fiscal rules presents a fundamental governance dilemma. On one hand, forward-looking forecasts and fiscal rules are vital tools to enforce fiscal discipline, prevent short-term political opportunism, and reassure international financial markets regarding debt sustainability. Without target projections, budget planning risks becoming entirely reactive or vulnerable to unsustainable spending commitments. On the other hand, macroeconomic forecasting models rely on simplified theoretical assumptions and historical trends that perform poorly during structural economic shifts, geopolitical shocks, or trend reversals. Enshrining point-estimate forecasts into binding fiscal legislation, such as statutory debt brakes, creates significant policy risk. When a model underestimates growth or revenue, it triggers artificial austerity measures that suppress aggregate demand; conversely, overestimating growth encourages structural spending commitments that deteriorate public balance sheets. Furthermore, when forecasters apply unrecorded discretionary adjustments to their models, technical assumptions silently dictate political possibilities without public oversight or democratic accountability.

To establish a more resilient fiscal policy framework, Finland should reform its reliance on point-estimate forecasting in favor of adaptive, corridor-based management. Rather than binding fiscal targets and statutory adjustment obligations to single baseline projections, fiscal laws and budgetary frameworks should utilize confidence intervals and range-based targets. Automatic fiscal triggers should not be activated by minor forecast shifts; instead, policy adjustments should rely heavily on confirmed, trailing economic indicators—such as audited tax collection data and employment figures—with formal mid-term review clauses to adjust course as revised statistical data emerges. Furthermore, the Ministry of Finance and independent forecasting bodies should enforce full algorithmic transparency, publishing the precise code, assumptions, and discretionary overrides used in their models. Transitioning toward dynamic fiscal adjustments anchored in transparent methodologies and verified real-world metrics will safeguard fiscal responsibility while preventing unnecessary economic disruption caused by forecast errors.

title: Espoo Intends to Lay Off Employees Despite City's Financial Surplus
originalSummary: Kaupungin työntekijät ovat muutosneuvottelujen laajuudesta yllättyneitä ja järkyttyneitä.
analysis:
The city of Espoo is preparing to initiate organizational change negotiations in September 2024, targeting a reduction of approximately 300 full-time equivalent positions to achieve 10 million euros in annual personnel savings. Out of the city's 11,000 employees, roughly 3,000 in administration and support services will be subject to the negotiations, while 8,000 education and early childhood care personnel are explicitly excluded to safeguard statutory basic services. Labor unions representing municipal workers have expressed deep concern over job security, increased workplace stress, and the rationale for layoffs, noting that Espoo recorded a 111 million euro financial surplus in the previous fiscal year. Union representatives have also questioned why raising municipal tax rates has been ruled out. In response, Espoo Mayor Kai Mykkänen emphasized that operating expenses are growing structurally at 4 to 6 percent annually while revenues grow at only 1 to 2 percent. He noted that accounting surpluses are insufficient to cover the city's 400 million euro annual investment budget required for expanding infrastructure, new schools, and nurseries to support rapid population growth, alongside reduced state transfers.

The tension in Espoo illustrates a classic public finance dilemma: accounting surpluses do not necessarily indicate long-term structural balance, especially for fast-growing municipalities facing heavy capital expenditure requirements. Espoo's decision to insulate frontline educational personnel while targeting administrative and support overhead aligns with sound managerial principles that prioritize direct public service delivery. Structural spending growth that consistently outpaces revenue growth is unsustainable and would lead to severe debt accumulation if left unaddressed. However, implementing abrupt redundancies in administrative and support roles carries real risks of creating operational bottlenecks and shifting bureaucratic burdens onto remaining frontline staff, which can erode total organizational efficiency. Furthermore, executing workforce reductions during a general economic downturn increases local unemployment friction and public support costs.

To manage this transition effectively, Espoo should prioritize leveraging natural attrition, internal redeployment, and phased voluntary retirements over direct forced redundancies, particularly given that a significant portion of the city's municipal workforce is nearing retirement age. The municipal executive must pair headcount reductions with genuine process streamlining and thoughtful digital automation, ensuring that remaining workers are not overwhelmed by administrative spillover that ultimately leads to costly sick leaves. While maintaining competitive municipal tax rates is important for regional economic attractiveness, local decision-makers should maintain a balanced perspective where targeted internal efficiency gains are carefully measured against core service quality, utilizing minor revenue adjustments only if infrastructure and debt constraints threaten statutory service standards.

title: Tax Chief at Odds with Riikka Purra: Considers It Likely That Labor Taxation Will Tighten in the Next Parliamentary Term
originalSummary: Valtiovarainministeriön vero-osaston päällikkö arvioi, että on epätodennäköistä, että työn verotuksen tai arvonlisäveron korotukset jätettäisiin sopeutuksen ulkopuolelle.
analysis:
Terhi Järvikare, head of the tax department at the Finnish Ministry of Finance, has publicly diverged from Minister of Finance Riikka Purra regarding the necessary fiscal measures for the upcoming electoral term. While Purra and the Finns Party strongly oppose increases in labor and entrepreneurial taxation and advocate for achieving fiscal consolidation primarily through direct expenditure cuts, Järvikare argues that the magnitude of Finland's fiscal deficit makes tax hikes virtually unavoidable. Political consensus estimates that the government needs to adjust the public budget by 8 to 11 billion euros over four years to satisfy structural needs and comply with the European Union's excessive deficit procedure, which demands immediate, front-loaded fiscal tightening. Järvikare emphasizes that because the required adjustment is so substantial, revenue measures must target the largest tax bases—namely income taxation and value-added tax (VAT)—even though the current government has already raised the general VAT rate from 24 to 25.5 percent.

Evaluating this policy conflict highlights the deep structural trade-offs within Finnish public finance. Relying heavily on increases in labor taxation poses significant economic risks. High marginal tax rates on labor can dampen work incentives, reduce household disposable income, and curb domestic private consumption, ultimately dampening economic growth. In a country already characterized by high progressive income taxation, further tightening labor taxes can worsen brain drain and reduce labor market flexibility. Conversely, relying solely on spending cuts to close an 8 to 11 billion euro deficit is exceptionally difficult without dismantling core welfare services, especially given the rising expenditure driven by an aging population. Broad-based consumption taxes, such as VAT, generate substantial state revenue with relatively low administrative overhead, but they are inherently regressive and can squeeze consumer purchasing power if raised repeatedly in a short timeframe.

To navigate this fiscal bottleneck effectively, decision-makers should avoid relying on labor tax increases as a primary mechanism for budget balance. Increasing the tax burden on work directly undermines long-term economic dynamism and productivity growth, which are essential for long-run debt sustainability. Instead, the upcoming parliamentary term should prioritize deep structural spending reviews alongside targeted adjustments to non-labor tax bases. If revenue enhancements are required to satisfy EU fiscal frameworks, they should focus on broadening tax bases by eliminating distortive exemptions and loopholes rather than raising marginal tax rates on earned income. Combining strict discipline on public expenditure growth with tax neutrality on labor will provide the most sustainable path to stabilizing public debt without stifling the broader economy.

title: Analysis: This picture encapsulates our inability to take climate change seriously
originalSummary: Ilmastonmuutoksen aiheuttama uhka konkretisoituu kesä kesältä. Mutta päättäjät reagoivat uhkaan hitaasti, kirjoittaa Janne Toivonen.
analysis:
The article critically examines the inaction of global economic and political leadership in the face of escalating climate change, utilizing a striking photograph of tourists relaxing by a lake as a wildfire burns across the shore in Bordeaux as a metaphor for societal apathy. The author argues that while scientific consensus is clear and the economic toll of climate disasters—such as extreme heatwaves, agricultural losses, and severe floods—mounts into billions of euros, political decision-making remains paralyzed by political friction and fear of voter backlash. Public opinion polls consistently show that citizens largely support climate action, yet economic policies continue to actively support fossil fuels through environmentally harmful subsidies, such as tax exemptions for aviation, and slow, cautious carbon pricing mechanisms like the EU Emissions Trading System. Furthermore, the article critiques the traditional reliance on Gross Domestic Product (GDP) as a metric for success, pointing out that GDP growth is blind to the destructive nature of the economic activity generating it, as it treats disaster recovery costs and wartime production identically to constructive economic output. Right-wing populist parties are singled out as particularly resistant, often obstructing climate measures or denying the severity of the crisis, leading to a status quo where nations like Finland continue to allocate billions annually to environmentally harmful economic supports.

Evaluating the utility and efficiency of current economic policies regarding climate mitigation reveals a profound structural market failure. Subsidizing environmentally destructive activities—such as fossil fuel consumption and carbon-intensive transport—directly contradicts fundamental economic efficiency by creating negative externalities that are socialized onto taxpayers while privatizing the short-term gains of polluting industries. Economic theory dictates that prices should reflect the true social cost of goods and services; when carbon is underpriced or polluting sectors receive tax breaks, the market receives false signals that lead to the over-allocation of resources toward unsustainable practices. While political hesitation is frequently driven by concerns over competitiveness and short-term economic shocks, delaying structural transition merely compounds future costs, as evidenced by projections showing that unchecked climate change will inflict exponentially higher financial damages on public finances and infrastructure over the coming decades. Consequently, maintaining these policy frameworks is economically irrational over a medium- to long-term horizon, as the cumulative costs of disaster recovery and agricultural failure far outweigh the short-term costs of proactive decarbonization.

To address this systemic policy failure, governments must urgently dismantle the economic incentives that favor fossil fuels and align fiscal policy with empirical climate science. The most direct and necessary course of action is the systematic phasing out of environmentally harmful subsidies, beginning with the removal of tax exemptions for aviation and other fossil-fuel-reliant sectors, thereby correcting market distortions without requiring complex new interventions. Simultaneously, carbon pricing mechanisms must be expanded and accelerated, eliminating exemptions for heavy industry to ensure that polluters bear the full financial burden of their emissions, which will naturally drive innovation and efficiency through market incentives. Finally, governance frameworks must evolve beyond the single-minded pursuit of traditional GDP growth by integrating ecological indicators and genuine progress indicators into national budgeting and economic planning. By redefining economic success to account for environmental depreciation and sustainability, policymakers can overcome the current paralysis and steer public policy away from short-sighted appeasement toward long-term macroeconomic resilience.

title: EU Outsources the Prevention of Unauthorized Entry to Partner Countries, and It Comes with Problems
